title: To counter AI misinformation, invest in skills, literacy
where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Tim Curtis, UNESCO)
syllabus: GS3 › Internal security: role of media and social networking sites; Cyber security; Science and technology: AI · GS2 › Important international institutions (UNESCO); Education (digital and media literacy); Elections · GS4 › Ethics in media and technology; Role of education in inculcating values
summary: UNESCO's South Asia head argues that laws and AI labels cannot keep pace with AI-made misinformation; India must build media and information literacy (MIL) for all, with platforms, newsrooms and creators sharing the job.
ideas: From access to judgement: generative AI makes convincing fakes cheap, so the question is no longer how to find information but how to judge what is reliable. Media and information literacy (MIL) is the answer.
GS3 · AI and misinformation
With generative AI making fakes cheap, the challenge has shifted from accessing information to judging it, which makes media and information literacy essential.
Connectivity is not capability: India has over a billion internet subscribers, but few can navigate the information space; platforms reward emotionally charged content, which deepens polarisation.
GS3 · Digital divide / social media
India's billion internet users show connectivity, not capability: only 18% of adults can file a cybercrime complaint online.
Misinformation does most harm in crises and elections, when people most need reliable information.
GS3 internal security · GS2 elections
Misinformation is most dangerous in crises and elections, as out-of-context flood videos in Nepal and a fake AI audio in Slovakia's election show.

Laws and labels are not enough: labelling AI content helps, but no law or detection tool can match the speed of synthetic content; people need skills, through trained teachers, local-language materials, and outreach beyond classrooms to rural people, women and persons with disabilities.
GS3 · Way forward / GS2 education
No law or detection tool can keep pace with AI fakes; lasting defence lies in citizens' skills, taught in local languages and beyond classrooms.

'We All Play a Part': platforms must be transparent about algorithms, label synthetic media and moderate beyond English and Hindi; newsrooms must explain how they verify; creators need verification skills and ethics.
GS3 governance · GS4 media ethics
Countering misinformation is a shared duty: transparent platforms, newsrooms that explain verification, and creators trained in ethics.
MIL is an investment in democracy: children grow up in AI-shaped feeds before they can question them, so MIL builds critical thinking, social trust and collective resilience.
GS2 democracy · Essay
Media literacy is not just safe technology use; it is an investment in critical thinking, social trust and democratic resilience.
keywords: Ability to access, understand, evaluate and share information responsibly
Media and information literacy is the most durable defence against AI-made misinformation.
AI that creates realistic text, images, audio and video
Generative AI has made synthetic media cheap and convincing.

Platforms built for attention amplify emotionally charged and divisive content.

Policing harmful content in all Indian languages
In multilingual India, moderation must work beyond English and Hindi.
Real evidence dismissed as fake because fakes are common
The spread of deepfakes lets people dismiss genuine footage as fake: the liar's dividend.
A society's shared ability to resist manipulation
MIL builds collective resilience against disinformation.

trend.t: Social media has moved through the papers from a tool of terror (ISIS recruitment 2015, non-state actors 2016) to a security challenge (social media and encryption 2024) to fake news and its regulation (IT Rules 2026). GS4 has added the ethics of social media (2025) and of AI (2024, 2026).
trend.watch: Social media and misinformation have come in four GS3 papers and in GS4 2025, and AI in 2023, 2024 and 2026. AI-driven misinformation joins both threads and is a must-study topic.

title: Climate justice needs quicker compensation: first Loss and Damage payout to Nepal
syllabus: GS3 › Environment; Disaster management · GS2 › International institutions; India's neighbourhood · GS4 › Ethical issues in international funding
context: The UN's Fund for Loss and Damage has allocated $21.6 million (about Rs 190 crore) to Nepal, nearly two months after devastating floods. It is the first time the Fund has earmarked a grant for a disaster-affected nation. The Indian Express argues the episode should become a case study for reforming the Fund.
ideas: Loss and damage is compensation, not charity, because it rests on responsibility for climate change.
GS3 climate · GS2 global governance
Loss and damage finance is compensation owed, not charity, because it rests on responsibility for emissions.
Speed is justice: delays raise hardship and rebuilding costs, especially for poor countries.
GS3 DM · GS4 fairness
Delayed climate compensation is justice denied: it raises hardship and rebuilding costs.
Money is short: $822 million pledged, about a third of pending claims.
GS3 · Climate finance
The Loss and Damage Fund has only $822 million pledged, about a third of pending claims.
keywords: Climate harm beyond what mitigation and adaptation can prevent
Loss and damage covers harm beyond what mitigation and adaptation can prevent.
Sharing climate burdens by responsibility and capacity
Climate justice demands that burdens be shared by responsibility and capacity.
Common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities
India's climate diplomacy rests on CBDR-RC: common but differentiated responsibilities.
Those who cause harm bear its cost
The polluter pays principle makes loss and damage a duty of high emitters.
data: Nepal emits barely 0.1% of global emissions yet suffers some of the worst climate disasters.
Pledged to the Fund, about a third of pending claims
Pledges of $822 million cover only about a third of pending loss-and-damage claims.
examples: Nepal: low emitter, high impact
Barely 0.1% of emissions, yet among the hardest hit
GS4
GS4 · Fairness
Nepal, a low emitter facing high losses, shows why climate justice is a moral question.
Avalanche-triggered floods in Nepal
An ice-and-rock avalanche set off flash floods and wrecked hydropower plants
Disaster answers
Nepal's avalanche-triggered floods show cascading Himalayan hazards that destroy infrastructure.
pyqs: Loss-and-damage finance as part of climate commitments: first grant, $822 million pledged against far larger claims.
Nepal's avalanche-triggered floods as a Himalayan climate hazard with cross-border lessons.
Nepal lost at least 10% of its hydropower facilities: infrastructure in fragile terrain.
Nepal's case shows who pays for 'development' driven by greed: low emitters, high losses.
links: Related Explained (Telegram): Why Rs 190 crore payout to Nepal matters
summary: The UN Fund for Loss and Damage made its first grant, to flood-hit Nepal; the Indian Express says payouts must be faster and the Fund reformed.
evolution: Fund for Loss and Damage created at COP27, after a nearly three-decade campaign by vulnerable nations.
First grant earmarked, to Nepal; developed countries insisted it is an exception, not a precedent.
COP31 begins in Antalya, Turkey, with compensation on the agenda.

title: Ahead of Cyclone Arnab, Andhra evacuates pregnant women; Odisha deploys ministers
syllabus: GS3 › Disaster management · GS4 › Care ethics of the state; Compassion towards the weaker sections
context: With the IMD forecasting landfall of Cyclone Arnab on the Andhra Pradesh coast on 28 October, Andhra Pradesh began evacuating vulnerable people, and Odisha banned sea fishing and tourist entry in six districts.
ideas: Good preparedness protects the most vulnerable first, before landfall.
GS3 · DM best practice
Good preparedness protects the most vulnerable first, before landfall.
Many layers act together: early warning, NDRF and SDRF teams, school closures, fishing bans and ministers on the ground.
GS3 · Coordinated response
Early warning, NDRF and SDRF teams, school closures and fishing bans work best together.
The state's ethics of care: planning for those who cannot protect themselves.
GS4 · Ethics of care
Evacuating pregnant women first reflects the state's ethics of care.
keywords: Preparedness aimed at saving every life
Cyclone preparedness should aim at zero casualties, protecting the most vulnerable first.
Identifying who is most at risk before a disaster
Vulnerability mapping lets the state protect those most at risk before disaster strikes.
Moral duty to attend to the needs of the vulnerable
The ethics of care asks administrators to put the most vulnerable first.
National and State Disaster Response Forces
NDRF and SDRF teams pre-positioned before landfall save lives.

GS4

pyqs: Proactive rather than reactive: 4,711 pregnant women moved to health centres before landfall.

Prioritising pregnant women before landfall: compassion and planning in disaster response.
summary: Before Cyclone Arnab's landfall, Andhra Pradesh moved 4,711 pregnant women to hospitals and Odisha sent eight ministers to the districts.

title: 'Godzilla' El Niño effects to be felt into 2027: decoding the WMO warning
syllabus: GS1 › Important geophysical phenomena; Climatology · GS3 › Food security; Disaster management
context: The World Meteorological Organization has warned that the intense 2026 El Niño will peak around year-end and affect weather well into 2027. It has already weakened India's southwest monsoon.
ideas: El Niño weakens the Indian monsoon, causing drought and heatwaves.
GS1 climatology · GS3 drought
El Niño weakens the Indian monsoon, bringing drought and heatwaves.
Effects into 2027 threaten food and water security and could push up fertiliser and fuel prices.
GS3 · Food security
The 2026 El Niño, lasting into 2027, threatens food and water security and could raise fertiliser and fuel prices.
keywords: Preparing farming and water systems to withstand dry years
Drought-proofing farming and water systems is the answer to recurring El Niño years.
Rising food prices after a poor harvest
A weak monsoon feeds food inflation, hurting the poor most.
Farming that relies on rain, not irrigation
Monsoon-dependent agriculture leaves India exposed to every El Niño.
One shock triggering others: drought, prices, water
El Niño brings cascading risks: drought, prices, water shortage.
data: Share of India's annual rain from the southwest monsoon
The southwest monsoon brings about 70% of India's annual rainfall.
India's 2026 monsoon, the fourth driest since 2001
India's 2026 monsoon ended at 87% of the long period average, the fourth driest since 2001.
pyqs: El Niño as a drought driver: the 2026 monsoon ended at 87% of LPA.
WMO warning: an El Niño strong enough to weaken the monsoon and affect weather into 2027.
Effects into 2027 on food and water security.
summary: The WMO warns that this year's intense El Niño, which already weakened India's monsoon, will affect weather well into 2027.

Ended at 87% of LPA, the fourth driest since 2001.
